title: Hysterectomy: surgical removal of the womb
intro: A hysterectomy is an operation that removes the womb, sometimes together with the cervix, ovaries or fallopian tubes. It is performed for conditions such as fibroids, heavy bleeding, prolapse, endometriosis or cancer. Because it is permanent and ends the possibility of pregnancy, it is worth understanding the alternatives and what recovery involves.

sections.heading: Why it is done
paragraphs: Common reasons include fibroids, abnormal or heavy periods that do not respond to other treatment, endometriosis, adenomyosis, a prolapsed womb, chronic pelvic pain and cancers or precancerous changes of the womb, cervix or ovaries. Many of these problems have less invasive treatments, so a hysterectomy is often considered only after alternatives have been tried or discussed.

sections.heading: Types of operation
paragraphs: A hysterectomy may remove only the womb, called a total or subtotal procedure depending on whether the cervix is also taken, or include the ovaries and tubes. Removing the ovaries before menopause causes immediate menopause symptoms and has long-term effects, so this is discussed carefully.

The operation can be done through the vagina, through keyhole surgery, or through a larger cut in the abdomen. The best route depends on the reason, the size of the womb and your health. Keyhole and vaginal routes usually mean shorter hospital stays and quicker recovery.

sections.heading: Risks
paragraphs: Like any major operation, a hysterectomy carries risks such as bleeding, infection, blood clots, anaesthetic problems and injury to the bladder, bowel or ureters. Some women have changes in bladder function or in sexual experience. Most women feel their symptoms improve, and they are glad that heavy bleeding or pain has stopped.

sections.heading: Recovery
paragraphs: Hospital stay is typically one to a few days. Expect tiredness and discomfort for several weeks. Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity as advised, take short walks to prevent clots, and follow instructions on intercourse and bathing. Most women return to usual activities within about six weeks, though this varies with the type of surgery.
Contact your doctor if you have heavy bleeding, fever, severe pain, or swelling and redness of a leg. Emotional reactions, including grief or relief, are normal, and support is available.

sections.heading: Questions to settle before surgery
paragraphs: Ask about alternatives, whether the ovaries will be kept, effects on hormones and sexual life, and what recovery will involve. You are entitled to take time and to ask for a second opinion before agreeing.

examples.title: Exploring alternatives
examples.text: Imagine you have heavy periods and your doctor suggests a hysterectomy. You could ask whether a hormonal coil, medicines, or a smaller procedure might help first, and what the benefits and drawbacks of each are.

examples.title: Planning recovery
examples.text: Suppose your surgery is scheduled in two weeks. You might arrange help with shopping and childcare, prepare easy meals and ask your employer about the time off you are likely to need.
